stimulus.text:
| Part of one township | Lots | Acres | What happened to it |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Whole township | 36 | 23,040 | Six miles square, divided into 36 lots of 640 acres each |
| Reserved for the United States | 4 (lots 8, 11, 26, 29) | 2,560 | Held for future sale |
| Reserved for public schools | 1 (lot 16) | 640 | Income from the lot paid for schools |
| Offered for sale at auction | 31 | 19,840 | Sold for at least $1 an acre; smallest purchase one lot ($640) |
stimulus.source_note: Table drawn from the Land Ordinance of 1785 (Journals of the Continental Congress, May 20, 1785). Public domain.

primary_sources: Land Ordinance of 1785 (Journals of the Continental Congress, May 20, 1785)

stem: The table shows the smallest purchase was one lot — 640 acres for $640. What does that price tell a historian about who could buy land at first?

options.text: Most ordinary settlers could not afford it, so speculators bought first
Ordinary farm families could easily afford a lot of their own
options.misconception: Background: $640 in cash was far beyond what most ordinary farm families held.

options.text: The government gave the land away free
options.misconception: The table says land sold for at least $1 an acre, not free.

options.text: Land sales quickly paid off the national debt
options.misconception: Background: early land sales brought only a small revenue, not a quick payoff of the debt.

rationales.A: Background from the books: few settlers had the capital for a $640 purchase, so early sales favored speculators and land companies, and the debt-ridden government received only a small revenue from its lands at first.
rationales.B: Background: $640 in cash was far beyond most ordinary farm families in the 1780s.
rationales.C: The table says land sold for at least $1 an acre; it was not given away.
rationales.D: Background: early land sales brought only a small revenue, not a quick payoff of the war debts.
rationales.general:
1. Read the price. The smallest purchase was one lot: 640 acres for $640.
2. Background: few ordinary settlers held $640 in cash in the 1780s.
3. Background: early buyers were mainly speculators and land companies with capital.
4. The price was set high to raise revenue, and the cost fell hardest on ordinary families.
Remember: a high minimum price decides who gets the land, not just how much it costs.
